body.heading: Losing is the price of playing
paragraphs: Every game worth playing has a loser. That is not a flaw — it is the deal. Without the chance of losing, winning would mean nothing, and the game would be a puzzle you solve once and put away.

The sting of losing usually comes from surprise: we expected to win, or we were winning until the last card. Naming that feeling helps. "I'm annoyed because I was so close" is a much easier feeling to carry than a vague, grumpy mood that spoils the evening.

body.heading: Small habits that soften a loss
paragraphs: First, congratulate the winner — sincerely, and straight away. It is the fastest way to close the game in your own head, and it makes the table a nicer place for everyone. Second, find one thing you did well, even in a loss: a clever move, a good guess, a comeback that nearly worked.

Third, keep the stakes friendly. Play for the laugh, the story and the rematch, not for pride. And if a loss still stings, say so lightly — "That one hurt, well played" — and ask for a rematch. The best players are rarely the ones who win most; they are the ones everyone wants to play again.

description: Nobody plays to lose — but everyone loses sometimes. A few small habits can turn a loss from a sting into something you actually enjoy.
